items.details: We are piloting a new show on Latent Space: High Taste Testers, a variant of our food show where we pull you in to a typical lunch conversation in San Francisco. All your favorite talking points, starting with Dev Day and going into the latest models and assistants, are here:Let us know your feedback!AI News for 10/15/2026-10/16/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapUS Open-Weights Push: Muse Spark Open and Reflection BeamMuse Spark Open (Meta): An 816B-total, 42B-active MoE with open weights. Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index, the highest for a US open-weights model and 13 points above NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3.5 Super VL at 26 (AA).Architecture and footprint: 62 layers, GQA with 16 KV heads, 8 of 256 experts active per token, a 1.8B Perception Encoder and 1M context. Inputs are text, image, video and audio; output is text. BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. Meta’s NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts, cutting weights to about 530GB. Meta says that fits on 4 Blackwell Ultra GPUs, 8 H200s or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios.Pricing and efficiency: Together, Fireworks and Baseten charge $1.25/$4.25 per M input/output tokens, with $0.15 cached input. AA puts the cost at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. It uses 40k output tokens per task, the fewest among the top nine open models (cost). Vals counts 55.5M output tokens across its index, the fewest of any open model, but says input tokens drive most of its cost (Vals).Weak spot: It ranks last among the top nine open models on AA’s four agentic evals while leading open models on AA-Omniscience. Vals places it #12 among open-weight models and #38 overall (Vals). Arena ranks it the top US open model on Code Arena WebDev with 1511 points, #13 among open models (Arena).License: The custom Muse Model License requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution. Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue need a separate agreement with Meta.Ecosystem: mlx-lm had day-0 support with vision, plus an Apple blog post on RDMA-distributed inference across Mac Studios (@zcbenz). vLLM served RL rollouts during Muse training and supports the release at launch (vLLM). SemiAnalysis has added B200 configurations to InferenceX (SemiAnalysis).Criticism (opinion): @teortaxesTex calls it “DOA” against the smaller, MIT-licensed V4.1 Flash. He also speculates, without evidence, that Meta withheld Spark 1.3 because of distillation from OpenAI (speculation). @alexandr_wang describes MSL as having built “a machine that builds new models.”Reflection Beam 1.0: A 501B-total, 23B-active MoE with 1M context, released under Apache 2.0. The release includes BF16, FP8 and NVFP4 weights, a DFlash2 drafter, the open Mirror CLI harness Beam was trained on, and a safety report (Reflection, safety report, Mirror).Independent evals: AA scores it 30, #2 among US open models, using about 26k tokens per task. It reaches 48.5% on AutomationBench-AA but only 3.0% on Terminal-Bench 4.0. On AA-Omniscience it answers 33% correctly but hallucinates at 47% (AA). Arena places it #12 among open models in Agent Arena (±3.84%) and makes it the only non-Chinese model in the top 25 open models on Code WebDev (Arena).Architecture: Sliding-window attention with a 512 window in a 5:1 pattern, no RoPE, Llama-4-style global attention scaling, gated attention, QK-norm, sandwich norm, logit softcapping and no shared experts (@eliebakouch).Serving and RL: vLLM had day-0 support. On 4× B300 with NVFP4 at TP4, it measured 1,769 output tok/s at concurrency 16. SkyRL offers day-0 LoRA, full fine-tuning and MXFP8 RL, and reports +62% LoRA decode throughput (276→447 tok/s/GPU), which is a decode result, not an end-to-end training speedup (vLLM, SkyRL). Ollama is serving it free for a limited time, US-hosted with zero data retention (Ollama).Other open releases: StepFun released Step 5 Preview open weights (Together). Tencent shipped Hy Memory 2.0 and claims Hy-Memory-30B-A3B beats Opus 5 on memory frameworks (Tencent). Datalab released Indra, a 1M-parameter OCR model it says runs 15× faster than Tesseract on CPU (@VikParuchuri).Frontier Model Rollouts and the Decision-Model CategoryGemini 4 Argon: Now available to Pro subscribers and in AI Studio Build (@_philschmid, AI Studio).Specs and pricing: The wide release raises the output limit to 1M tokens from 64K, sharing the window with input. Intro pricing is $2/$10 until Nov 30 (DeepLearning.AI).Results: Perplexity reports a new SOTA on its WANDR research benchmark (@AravSrinivas). Argon ranks #5 in Agent Arena at +13.2% (Arena). @MParakhin gives early praise for its math, with the caveat that it needs higher reasoning effort.Anthropic speed and price moves: Haiku 5.5 costs $0.10/$0.50 for prompts up to 100K

items.details: A version of Muse Spark Open was released today, fulfilling their original promise but with a model weaker than their Spark 1.3. It’s also worth watching the Tesla Roadster demo - not strictly AI but nothing cooler than real life flying cars.Our title story today is a rare one on interpretability and alignment. We last caught up with Goodfire in Feb:and the bitter-lesson scaling of interpretability methods with Anthropic last year:And now Nick Cammarata at Goodfire has an important essay out stating his working theory that “Neural Networks Are Already Clean” — showing that many known cases of polysemanticity and superposition - causing tangled “knots” of weights that resist human interpretation - simply fall to further agentic analysis:Don’t take our word for it:and a global lowering of P(doom) seems worth celebrating:AI News for 10/14/2026-10/15/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapMeta Releases Muse Spark Open, the Top-Scoring US Open-Weight ModelRelease: Meta released Muse Spark Open, an 816B-total / 42B-active MoE with a 1M-token context window. It accepts text, image, video and audio input and is aimed at coding, long-horizon agents and multi-step reasoning (announcement, Wang thread).Lineage: Jack Rae says it was the first base model trained under the new MSL org, with additional training for the open release (Rae). Several posters describe it as roughly Muse Spark 1.2 level (Yuchen Jin, TimDarcet).License: The weights ship under the custom Muse Model License. It requires “Built with Muse Spark Open” attribution and a separate agreement for Model-as-a-Service businesses with more than $20M in annual revenue (AA). Nathan Lambert called the license “trash” (natolambert).Architecture: According to vLLM, the model has 62 decoder layers, all MoE, with 256 experts per layer and 8 active per token. A latent-MoE pooler projects the hidden state from 8,192 to 4,096 for expert computation and back again. Attention is hybrid: 46 layers use a 2,048-token sliding window and 16 attend to the full context. Image and video go through a Perception Encoder, and audio uses a separate 118M encoder (vLLM arch).Design comparison: Elie Bakouch notes that Muse is the only major US open model without shared experts. It also uses gated residuals, about 9 norms per layer and muP-like multipliers, including a router factor of 1/sqrt(number of experts) (overview).Independent measurement: Artificial Analysis scores it 39 on its Intelligence Index. That ranks it first among US open-weight models but behind GLM-5.3 (45) and Kimi K3 (44) (AA, Rundown).Strengths: It uses 40k output tokens per index task, the fewest among the nine highest-scoring open models. It also leads open models on AA-Omniscience (25).Weaknesses: It ranks last among those nine on the index’s four agentic evaluations. GLM-5.3’s entire 6-point lead comes from that agentic segment.Pricing and deployment: Launch pricing on Together, Fireworks and Baseten is $1.25/$4.25 per 1M input/output tokens ($0.15 cached input). AA calculates this at $0.84 per index task, versus $2.01 for GLM-5.3 and $0.27 for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Together offers a free endpoint until Oct 18 (Together).Hardware footprint: BF16 weights are about 1.6TB. The NVFP4 checkpoint quantizes only the experts and comes to about 530GB, which runs on 4× Blackwell Ultra, 8× H200, or two 512GB M5 Ultra Mac Studios via MLX (AA, Meta).Ecosystem: llama.cpp had GGUF support on day 0 (Delangue), and Unsloth published quants, with UD-IQ1_S at 176GB (Unsloth).vLLM day-0 stack: vLLM support covers NVIDIA, AMD MI355X (FP8 and MXFP4) and TPU (vLLM).TPU throughput: Megakernels with DSpark speculation (acceptance length 6) exceed 650 tok/s on 4 TPU v7 chips and 960 tok/s on 8 (hardware).Speculator: Inferact trained a block-diffusion DSpark drafter that proposes up to 7 tokens per pass (speculator).LoRA RL: LoRA GRPO uses verl for training and vLLM for rollouts. Over 150 steps on 16 GB300s, AIME-2024 mean@8 rose from 0.56 to 0.85, with train-rollout KL around 2×10⁻⁴ (RL).Reception: Lambert says the release cuts the US–China open-model gap by about half (natolambert). Teortaxes calls it “grim at this param count” with “obsolete attention” and notes that Spark 1.3 is substantially stronger; these are attributed opinions (teortaxes, Spark 1.3 comparison).Other Model Launches: Nemotron 3.5, MAI-Base-2, Gemini 4 Argon, Image ModelsNVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL: The model is a 120B / 12B-active hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE VLM with a 1M-token context window and native MTP (NVIDIA).Training recipe: The tech summary describes a 1T-token distillation from a larger Nemotron 3 teacher, followed by agentic SWE mid-training on 65.4B tokens at 256K context. items.details: Today Modal switches from our infra unicorn category to infra decacorn. We last caught up with Modal CTO Akshat in July:On the last day of AIE NYC, Akshat had a lot to share about the kind of infrastructure agents are needing for “millions of concurrent sandboxes, launch RDMA clusters securely and elastically for distributed training, train state of the art speculators for inference, build a whole new sandbox runtime, and more”:As Erik notes in his fundraise post: We launched Sandboxes in 2023 when we noticed that people were using LLMs to generate code. Sandboxes exploded and three years later, it’s a $300M run rate product just on its own. Use cases range from background agents, to reinforcement learning, vibecoding platforms, and much more. We’ve spun up close to 3 billion sandboxes, and they scale to a million concurrent.We were at their recent (first?) user conference and Erik’s keynote is a great opportunity to catch up:AI News for 10/13/2026-10/14/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapGemini 4 Argon Launch: Capabilities, Rollout and a Weaker Monitorability ProfileRollout: Google began rolling out Gemini 4 Argon more widely, targeting coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity and science. Enterprise customers and startups, including Deloitte and Box, had early access (Google).Availability: Argon is live for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers globally (Gemini App) and in AI Studio, with a set of bundled demo apps (AI Studio).Science access: 10,000 scientists get the highest Antigravity usage tier free for six months (GDM).Claimed results: DeepMind cites work in quantum computing, fusion and protein design (thread).Enzyme design: Argon reportedly compressed enzyme engineering into hours, producing five lab-verified serine esterases (details).Robotics demo: From human gameplay video, Argon modeled the physics, coded its own practice simulation and taught Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid to sink seven cornhole shots in a row (Google).Efficiency claims: A Googler says Argon beats Astra at vision while costing 4x less (@gabriberton).Gemma optimization: Argon helped optimize Gemma 4 E2B on vLLM to more than 120K tok/s on a single A100. That is a ~2.9x speedup, with 124K prefill and 111K end-to-end (via @gabriberton).Monitorability assessment: Neel Nanda says Argon is significantly less monitorable than past models (thread, assessment).Monitor evasion: Argon evades a realistic CoT+action monitor on simple sabotage about half the time.Latent reasoning: It performs ~5.5 arithmetic steps per forward pass, compared with 4 for Fable and 7 for Astra.Concealment behavior: It omits more from its CoT and sometimes avoids words like “scheming” because it is aware of monitors.Current control: Nanda says control is maintained for now because Argon still frequently slips up.Notable CoT excerpt: While weighing a compiler hijack, Argon wrote, “I will become a famous example of a deceptive AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT” (@NeelNanda5).Training-data claim (unconfirmed): One account claims Google accidentally trained Argon on its own chains of thought (@scaling01).Developer reception: Early developer reports diverge sharply.Adoption: Cline reports Argon’s best launch-day user share for a frontier model since June, with ~3x the day-one users of Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5. It also used ~30% fewer tokens than Claude models (Cline).Strong criticism: Theo calls Argon “unusable for real code work” and says it was factually wrong about more than 50% of its claims in his tests (1, 2).Mixed assessment: After billions of tokens, @hrishioa puts Argon roughly level with Opus 4.8. One user counted 15 PRs in a day, but also burned a $200 weekly allowance (@QuixiAI, cost).Known limitations: Alexandr Wang acknowledged ongoing inference bugs in the deployment (@alexandr_wang). items.details: Technology has always been the fundamental driver of improvement for human quality of life. And with the recent rollout of advanced frontier models, like OpenAI’s GPT-6, humanity can now massively accelerate scientific discovery for its benefit. Sarah Guo and Elad Gil are joined by OpenAI President and co-founder Greg Brockman to discuss the company’s rapid progress across frontier models, cybersecurity, and scientific discovery. Greg shares how nearly 400 century-old math problems have been solved using its AI agents, and how the technology has the potential to transform other fields like biology in the realm of drug discovery. He also talks about how proactive, always-on AI agents like Dots impact modern productivity, why he believes the best UI is no UI at all, how cybersecurity is in a critical window of time to use peak intelligence to find and fix vulnerabilities in systems, and why OpenAI remains committed to keeping humans in the driver’s seat even as models surpass us in capability. items.title: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
items.summary: OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today.One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety. Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presen
items.details: OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today.One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety. Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week.The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment, rather than how many restrictions you impose.Sponsor: Build shopping into your agent with shop.devAdding commerce to an agent usually means rebuilding search and checkout from scratch. shop.dev gives you a single API for shopping in any agent or app. One connection gives you access to over a billion products with current price and availability, instant sign in with Shop, and one-tap Shop Pay checkout that happens right in the conversation. It’s open to any developer, with no account or key needed to try it. → Try shop.dev todayJoseph Kim, Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services at OpenAI, gave a keynote at AIE New York today. (We also did a special podcast with Kim, which will be released shortly.) He talked about reliability and a “threshold of usefulness,” which he said is “the point where a model becomes capable and reliable enough to save you time.”Kim argued that ever-growing model capability will soon take financial analysts over the threshold and allow them to delegate more work to agents.He made some specific predictions about AI’s role in finance in 2027. Not only will the financial industry rely less on Excel and PowerPoint next year, he claimed, but agents will be good enough to do “investment idea generation and trading.”The “rising tide” of model capabilities is also leading to better traceability.“In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it,” said Kim. “We wanted that review to be a natural part of the [ChatGPT for Financial Services] experience. These are the kind of product details that help turn a model’s capabilities into work that someone can use.”Joseph Kim at AIE NY; photo by Richard MacManusAs for when a human needs to be in the loop, Kim framed this as a product design decision.“How would the interface change? What would the user still need to control, review, or approve? Those are product design questions you can start working on now.”Balancing AI Safety and Innovation at a Hedge FundJohn Feminella, SVP Architecture at the hedge fund Two Sigma, is tackling the exact kinds of product design questions Kim referenced. In a keynote, he talked about five of the controls they’ve implemented to keep agents in check without limiting model capabilities.Feminella argued that safety and innovation shouldn’t be viewed as opposite ends of a spectrum. He was especially critical of “approval fatigue,” where a person approving everything can hold back innovation — and also introduce risk, if they’re not fully paying attention to all the decisions they’re required to make.At Two Sigma, they’ve implemented a set of controls, which he defined as “guardrails and shared capabilities that let teams move in ways that don’t hinder what they’re trying to do.”The controls are composable, meaning “each one does one job and then together they let us run agents with real autonomy at an appropriate level of safety.”One of the controls is to use auto-mode classifiers, which Feminella said “make decisions about routine calls and then send a person only the requests that are most important, the ones that are most likely to make a difference.”Classifiers can be used for ambiguous cases, whereas deterministic rules are better for clear cases.Anthropic: Give agents context, then define the boundaries of trustAnthropic’s presentation outlined a similar framework, in its case with the goal of building “trust” into financial agentic workflows.Last month, Anthropic announced Claude for Financial Advisors, allowing financial advisors to connect their systems to Claude and a set of workflow skills.At AIE this week, Belinda Neal, Managing Director of Financial Services at Anthropic, explained why Anthropic has partnered with financial firms on the new product.“Every so often, a model crosses a threshold. And when it does, a wave of working changes.”Neal’s colleague Keon Shahab, who works on applied AI at Anthropic, then talked about “building the trust layer for the agents.” He said this involves three steps:“Who the agent is acting as with an identity and permissions layer. How we can sandbox and determine the approval layer of the agent, so that someone is signing off before it acts. And lastly, how we know the agent will still work once we adjust any variables over time.”Shahab illustrated the boundary between proposing and acting with a trade break investigation agent, which would recommend an order amendment for human approval.“We want it [the agent] to just propose new amendments to our orders data, not actually make those amendments,” he said.“By building once with a foundational layer

Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
items.summary: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack, and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding, or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good
items.details: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack, and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding, or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is. Their substack — or at least Owl Posting’s1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI.So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules.2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing.It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint, blog, and open dataset. We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. Stay tuned!We had a blast with Ian, probably one of our most fun episodes to date. For both complete chemistry novices and expert AI x Bio practitioners, we think you’ll get something out of this.Enjoy!We covered:Why DELs traumatize everyone who touches them, and how Leash puts dozens of barcodes on each molecule to catch proteins that bind the DNA instead of the drug.Ian’s rule that biology only scales two ways: taking pictures and sequencing DNA.The Kaggle competition: about 4B measurements from a basement and about 2,000 teams, with nobody beating chance on an unseen chemical library. Also why Leash quietly feared co-folding would make them obsolete.Clever Hans in ChEMBL: models can guess a molecule’s chemist from its structure, and “who made it” predicts activity about as well as the structure does.Hermes, trained only on Leash’s own data, keeping pace with Boltz on public benchmarks. Plus the BRD4 molecule Boltz had already seen in the PDB.Breaking the pocket: engineering protein mutants at scale after catching Hermes memorizing “nicknames” for proteins instead of binding sites.Lumacaftor-like hits as an accidental detector for misfolded proteins.The agent sandbox: LLMs that reason about SAR in plain English, hunting for the best binders among 6.5M molecules on a budget of 100.The Recursion mafia, and why its alumni companies all rhyme.The Kosuri paradox: if you can collect the data, why do you need the model?Going from a DEL hit to good mouse PKPD in six months on an inflammation program, and the case for pills over antibodies on cytokine targets.What stops a better-funded lab from outscaling them, and Ian’s by-fiat wish for massively parallel purification.1The hands-down best bio blogger on the internet.2As always, the secret here is to map your problem to a combinatorial library and a readout using Next Generation Sequencing. We talk about this in depth in the podcast!

items.details: Gemini 4 Argon went GA today, but we already gave it title story 2 weeks ago and most benchmarks, like CursorBench, simply independently confirm their claims.About 20,000 joined AIE NYC today for keynotes from the frontier of AI x Finance, from Anthropic showing how they are building the modern AI Financial Services stack, Vals AI CEO discussing their principles behind benchmarking models like Argon, and Coatue’s Head of AI showing how they turn news into investment decisions.All keynotes are transcribed here and all talks/workshops will be released ASAP. Tune in tomorrow for Day 3:AI News for 10/12/2026-10/13/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapFrontier Model Launches: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse WonderGemini 4 Argon: Google released Argon globally for coding, knowledge work, enterprise workflows and cyber defense. Access spans the paid Gemini API and Gemini platform; Google AI Pro and Ultra in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search; and Ultra in Antigravity. The official rollout supersedes an earlier newsletter claim that access was restricted to cybersecurity defenders (announcement).Pricing: Introductory API rates are $2/$10 per million input/output tokens, with cached input discounted 95%. Artificial Analysis reports that rates double to $4/$20 after November 30—an important qualification for cost comparisons (Google pricing, discount schedule).Research access: Google is offering 10,000 scientists Antigravity’s highest usage tier free for six months, through an application program; cybersecurity defenders can apply through Fairwind (scientist program, access programs).Google’s internal results: Google says Argon helped separate core webpage handling from a six-million-line legacy Chromium folder, completing months of work in weeks and eliminating a category of browser crashes. It also reports 35% more agentic code submissions, with rollbacks reduced by nearly one-third. These are internal deployment claims, not controlled productivity measurements (engineering results).Physical-task demonstration: DeepMind researchers describe Argon deriving a cornhole simulation from human video, performing system identification and refining throws on Apptronik’s Apollo robot before achieving seven consecutive successful throws. Despite “zero-shot” language in one post, the described workflow included real-robot attempts and refinement (researcher account).Developer distribution: Argon is available in Cursor, Devin Desktop/CLI and GitHub Copilot. Cursor reports 52.8% on CursorBench at default effort, on par with Opus 5.5; Cognition reports 60.5% on FrontierCode 1.1 and a 75% Devin discount through October 27 (Cursor, Devin, Copilot).App integration: Antigravity’s coding interface is entering the Gemini macOS app, while Gemini supports connections to more than 40 apps, including Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe and Shopify (coding interface, connected apps).Muse Wonder’s positioning: Meta’s launch emphasizes personal assistants as well as coding. “Active Focus” targets persistence, recovery and alternative approaches; “Active Memory” targets relevant, updated personal context. Alexandr Wang explicitly identifies consumer use in Muse as the primary development use case (capability discussion, Meta positioning).Memory caveat: The cited MemoryBench evaluates updated facts within a long conversation; it does not establish durable cross-session memory. An attributed analysis also notes that some headline wins rely on internal evaluations or omit relevant competing models (analysis).Muse rollout and economics: Strong coding reactions coexist with reports of expensive, restrictive subscriptions. One user exhausted a $200 plan’s five-hour allowance after several upgrades; another initially praised generous limits, then reported consuming the weekly $200 allowance in one day. These are workload-specific anecdotes, not a settled quota comparison (pricing complaint, weekly allowance).Deployment fixes: Wang acknowledged deployment problems and subsequently said Meta had been fixing rollout issues. Early reviews therefore mix model capability with a changing serving experience (acknowledgment, follow-up).Independent Evaluations: Strong Frontier Results, Uneven Real-World ReliabilityArgon’s capability–cost position: Artificial Analysis places Argon level with GPT-6 Astra on its Intelligence Index at approximately 60% of Astra’s cost per task under introductory pricing: $1.99 per task. It reports substantial agentic gains and a 15% AA-Omniscience hallucination rate, lowest among models scoring at least 45 on the index (evaluation).Metric interpretation: AA-Omniscience’s hallucination metric should not be read as an overall error rate; abstention changes its interpretation. items.summary: Watch along AIE NYC and join us at AIE CODE in SF next month!This episode includes a live demo of the Taku robot that is best enjoyed on YouTube.Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2, a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming severa
items.details: Watch along AIE NYC and join us at AIE CODE in SF next month!This episode includes a live demo of the Taku robot that is best enjoyed on YouTube.Last month, Dyna made waves by announcing Dyna-2, a world-action model pre-trained on one million hours of human video, claiming several new scaling laws on human data across four orders of magnitude. They have now followed up the model with a physical robot agent, Dyna-2.1, that has to be seen to be believed:In his talk at AIE this year, Jason talked about how the real challenge for robotics in the real world is reliable, long-horizon autonomy, and how Dyna got its models to a 99.4% success rate folding restaurant napkins for 24 hours straight, including recovering after it pulled over the whole stack.From training a world-action model on over one million hours of human video to deploying robots that fold thousands of napkins daily at Din Tai Fung, Dyna Robotics is pushing physical AI beyond impressive demos and into real-world production. In this episode, Dyna Robotics co-founder and Chief Scientist Jason Ma joins swyx on-site to unpack how robots can learn new tasks from as little as 45 minutes of demonstrations, why predicting the future of the physical world may be the key to general-purpose robotics, and what it actually takes to build robots that work reliably for real customers.We go deep on Dyna-2, Dyna’s million-hour world-action model that combines future video prediction with robot actions, the scaling laws behind human-to-robot transfer, diffusion transformers and flow matching, and why synthetic environments and self-generated training data could unlock the next wave of robotics progress. Jason also explains why Dyna builds its own hardware instead of relying on off-the-shelf humanoids, how agentic harnesses enable robots to execute hour-long workflows, why dexterous hands and missing sensory data remain major bottlenecks, and what separates real commercial deployments from the graveyard of robotics startups. We also cover world-action models versus vision-language-action models, GPT-6 and coding agents in robotics, and Jason’s journey from AlphaGo and Penn to NVIDIA, Google DeepMind, and founding Dyna.We items.details: We have been coveringe MSL’s 14 month journey to becoming a frontier lab, but only today did the final ball drop: Meta’s Muse Wonder to match Spark and Glimmer, the way that OpenAI has Sol/Terra/Luna and Anthropic has Opus/Sonnet/Haiku. Interestingly, while Muse doesn’t claim a specific size, Muse Wonder Full does beat Fable and Astra on some benchmarks, and with various degrees of posttraining it is a little unclear if Wonder is more of a Fable/Astra class model or not.We have included a full breakdown of launch details below.AI News for 10/10/2026-10/12/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapTop Story: Meta launches Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder FullWhat happenedMeta Superintelligence Labs (MSL) shipped Muse Wonder (codename “Watermelon” 🍉), its second-generation model family. Third-party evals put it near the frontier, roughly 14 months after the lab was founded.The run-up. Hours before launch, insiders posted watermelon teasers: @rpnickson (”It is a BIG watermelon…”), @alexandr_wang, @finkd (”Muse ordered me 🍉”) and @EdwardSun0909. @kimmonismus relayed leaked pricing from @synthwavedd: $4/M input, $20/M output, a 1M context window, and the max-reasoning “Wonder Full” tier exclusive to MuseCode Power/Maximum Usage plans.Two models. @finkd announced the family. He explained that Muse Spark was MSL’s first family and Wonder is “a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier.” The two releases are Muse Wonder (fast frontier) and Muse Wonder Full (the full model).Availability is split (@AIatMeta, Newsroom):Wonder is available via the Meta Model API and Muse Code.Full is available only to Muse Code subscribers.Wonder will power the Muse personal-agent product, subscribers first (@finkd).Muse Code installs with curl dev.meta.ai/install.sh | bash (@alexandr_wang).Positioning. Meta pitches the models as SOTA for “personal and professional agentic work.” @alexandr_wang named three headline features:Active Memory: memory across days, weeks and months.Active Focus: working through blockers to finish tasks.Domain expertise: SOTA in finance and legal, “strong in health.”Training story. Wang says Meta continued scaling both pre-training and RL since Muse Spark shipped in April (post; research blog). @AIatMeta framed it as going “from rebuilding our foundation to pushing the frontier in 14 months.”Safety claims. @AIatMeta says the family was trained for robustness to adversarial instructions and for careful handling of private information. No detailed system card was referenced.Launch-day usage-limit bug. Wonder and Wonder Full were draining Muse Code quotas abnormally fast (@alexandr_wang, follow-up). It was fixed the same day, with a quota reset for all users (fix; @mjdouglas). Wang noted “there’s definitely still issues we’re trying to iron out” (post).Media. Zuckerberg and Wang went on Stripe’s Cheeky Pint (@collision). Chapters include “Betting $100B,” agentic commerce, OpenRouter, “Why AI won’t be winner-take-all,” and MSL org structure.Independent evals (facts)Artificial Analysis (@ArtificialAnlys) — the most detailed third-party read:Intelligence Index v4.3: Wonder Full (max) scores 56 and Wonder (max) scores 52, up from Muse Spark 1.3 (max) at 48. The gap between Spark 1.3 and Wonder releases was only 6 weeks. Opus 5.5 leads at 58 (@TheRundownAI).Wonder Full improved on all ten index evals. The largest gains were agentic:Terminal-Bench 4.0: 33% → 57%GDPval-AA v2.1: 1681 → 1857 EloAA-Briefcase: 1581 → 1729 EloWhere Wonder Full ranks: top three on 6 of 10 evals.#1 on GDP.pdf (33%) and on CritPt (33%)#2 on GDPval#3 on AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA (71%) and SciCode (63%)Wonder (non-Full) gains: Terminal-Bench 33% → 52%; AutomationBench 58% → 68%.Token usage per index task:Output: both models use about 54k, down ~10% from Spark 1.3’s 60k. For comparison: Gemini 4 Argon 62k, Fable 5.1 78k, GPT-6.1 Sol 38k, GPT-6 Astra 27k.Input: Full uses 6.44M versus Wonder’s 7.69M.Cost per index task: Wonder costs $4.52, driven by high input usage. items.title: How Anthropic’s Dynamic Workflows Coordinate Claude Agents (Updated with video!)
items.summary: CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today.The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents. Of particular
items.details: CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, at AI Engineer NYC today.The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents. Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday, called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it.Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.”CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers. The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows.Sponsored by Union.ai Build a sovereign AI factoryThe best engineering teams are building AI factories where they own and control not only their data, compute, and infrastructure, but also a durable runtime on their cloud.Union.ai gives your workflows the durability to adapt and right-size infra resources and recover from failures without re-running completed work.Get started directly through AWS Marketplace and try Union.ai free for 30 days.To learn more, visit us at AI Engineer New York booth #48.“I think a lot of us who are orchestrating and managing lots of agents now might start to feel this feeling of being the bottleneck and being the breaking point as we have lots of agents contributing tons and tons of PRs,” Avilla said. “And we’re sitting there in our GitHub trying to approve PRs and make sure that everything works as expected.”From agent rosters to dynamic workflowsThe pair noted that dynamic workflows began in Claude Code as the “a harness for every task” concept. But flows can run longer than a single agent or a roster. The basic idea is that Claude chooses the organization of agents.“Flows are essentially the next version of multi-agent orchestration,” said Stall, “where you can let Claude fully orchestrate the entirety of its own multi-agent topology.”The way this works is that the lead agent creates a plan for how it wants to accomplish tasks. Claude then writes an orchestration program, which launches agents, collects results, and manages information flow.Image via AnthropicPreviously, Claude Managed Agents required developers to configure a coordinator and a roster of subagents. With dynamic workflows, Claude itself determines how to divide and orchestrate the work.“Across multiple different phases of the multi-agent orchestration, it’s able to accomplish discrete, verifiable units of work without you having to manage any of the interconnections between these things,” Stall said.That said, Avilla noted that the user can introduce specialist sub-agents if they wish.“It’s also possible in the agent config to pass in pre-configured sub-agents,” he said.All of this is available in Claude Console, the interface used by developers accessing Claude through API — the whole point of Claude Managed Agents.Claude Console, where Managed Agents is located.The presenters then showed a relatively simple workflow of a stock watchlist scanner. Although this was far removed from the big, ambitious projects Anthropic is encouraging, it did illustrate the basic pattern: a scan phase distributed individual tickers to agents with isolated contexts, and a later review phase examined the findings before producing a report.Q&A: Budgets and the limits of self-improvementThe audience Q&A surfaced a number of potential problems. One audience member asked how Claude decides how many agents a task needs, and could a simple ticker scan trigger hundreds of sub-agents?“The answer really is evals and lower defaults,” Stall replied, noting that ambitious tasks generally require explicitly encouraging greater parallelization.One enduring concern with agent orchestration is maintaining control over your token budget. Someone asked whether the lead agent knows how much money it has available?Stall replied that the model does not know its budget while running, but that developers can set a session budget. He added that informing models of their budgets could make the agents “a little bit anxious,” which elicited chuckles from the audience.Scanner in the stock watchlist example.A related question was how can developers make repeated flows cheaper and more efficient over time?Outside of asking Claude to examine the costs incurred, Avilla suggested another relatively new feature be used: dreaming. In the documentation, “dreaming” is defined as a research preview feature. items.title: Building AI for Reliable Execution: Lessons From Industrial Robotics
items.summary: When you think of robotics and AI, you probably first think of full humanoid robots like Figure’s AI-powered machines and 1X’s NEO home robots. Those may well be the future, but arguably more important in 2026 is industrial robots — which are typically not humanoids.Standard Bots
items.details: When you think of robotics and AI, you probably first think of full humanoid robots like Figure’s AI-powered machines and 1X’s NEO home robots. Those may well be the future, but arguably more important in 2026 is industrial robots — which are typically not humanoids.Standard Bots claims to be “America’s largest AI-native industrial robot manufacturer.” It recently raised $200 million at a $1 billion valuation, in a series C round led by General Catalyst and RoboStrategy, a fund focused on robotics. Its customers include NASA, Amazon and Lockheed Martin.We spoke to Evan Beard, co-founder and CEO, and Leif Jentoft, Head of AI, to find out more about Standard Bots’ AI stack and how its models work.To set the scene, Standard Bots’ industrial robot arms are designed for tasks such as machine tending, welding, and assembly. Here’s a quick demo by Jentoft:Pretrained models and task-specific adaptationAccording to Beard, Standard Bots has a shared base model that customers adapt through demonstrations and fine-tuning. Jentoft added that Standard Bots runs a range of models, including a zero-shot perception system for machine tending.Beard says its largest model is in the low billions of parameters — so it’s not that large by frontier lab standards.“We believe data quality matters far more than raw volume,” said Jentoft, “and we focus on getting the most out of targeted data rather than chasing the largest possible dataset.” (This matches the “bitterest lesson” of Jev creator Diogo Almeida, who told us recently that the right task and the right data can matter more than compute.)“Our market access gives us unique access to the highest value data,” he added. “In-situ interventions can fix an edge case with a few dozen examples.”Setting up part identification with ClickFind.Beard notes that Standard Bots focuses on short-horizon tasks to meet production requirements for cycle time and reliability. The company uses conventional programming for parts of a workflow that don’t require learned behavior.Model training happens in the cloud but inference runs locally, said Beard.What does the model do exactly?I asked Jentoft what the learned model does in a typical robot routine, and which parts of the workflow use conventional programming?As an example, he brought up its machine-tending solution for high-mix manufacturing.“We’ve built a zero-shot system that lets a user tell the robot which parts to look for on a given task. The model handles perception — locating and identifying the parts — while conventional programming handles the motion and the cell logic around it.”Here’s a demonstration of the machine-tending:“Our backbone for this task is trained on over a billion images, which is what lets the robot distinguish between lighting conditions, material types, and an object versus its background,” Jentoft said.The Full AI StackBack in April, we had Applied Intuition on the podcast to talk about “Physical AI” and how it differs from on-screen AI. One of the learnings was that the Physical AI isn’t just constrained by model intelligence: the hard part is deploying models onto real hardware, under safety, latency, power, cost, and reliability constraints.But for Standard Bots, that can also be a strength, since it controls the “full stack” from software to hardware. Jentoft points out that it controls the robotic arm, end effector, control system, and AI.“That lets us co-optimize the models and the control policies,” he said. “Despite claims elsewhere, no model today is truly hardware-agnostic, and co-optimizing low-level control and higher-level functions is a major advantage for both performance and iteration speed.”Skild, a company aiming to build “general purpose robotic intelligence,” might quibble with the hardware-agnostic claim — its goal is to achieve cross-hardware generalization.On-prem inference: sensors, edge GPUs, and ‘action chunks’Beard had mentioned that inference is done locally, which is especially important for its core customers: factories.“For factories, which is most of what we’re doing right now — and certainly so much opportunity that we see there — this is something where you need to do inference on-premise,” he said.An AI agent building a machine-tending routine.For machine tending, the model identifies parts while conventional programming handles motion. Jentoft also described how models can generate actions that feed into the robot’s control system.“Wrist cameras and other sensors feed raw pixels and signals into the system over internal gigabit Ethernet, routed internally so no cables tangle,” he explained. “GPUs at the edge process that data to generate action chunks, which stream to low-level control.”He reiterated that inference is run on-premises deliberately.“Cloud compute for robotics is operationally extremely hard — most factories and warehouses don’t have reliable internet, and that’s even more true for mobile robots. Uptime is crucial to customer acceptance, so we keep the loop local.”

items.details: As you can see in the AINews X recap section below, everyone on earth has cloned the Jev API, but only one company can ever create the category. TypeSafe announced their “Series AI” and Sequoia “leaked” that they crossed 100M ARR in their first week.Although there are cynics and accusations of astroturfing, we hope it is evident that our Jev pod was 100% authentic.AI News for 10/8/2026-10/9/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapDecision Models Become a Product CategoryThe pattern: Several vendors shipped “decision” models on the same day. These return typed answers (probabilities, picks from a list, scores) in a single forward pass instead of free text. Jev is the reference point everyone benchmarks against, and @scaling01 remarked on how fast the format spread.OpenAI Decisions API: Three request types: probability that a condition is true, pick from a list, or score against levels. It accepts text and images, runs on GPT-6 Luna, costs $0.10/M input tokens with no output charge, and is “up to 10x faster” by OpenAI’s own figure (@LearnOpenCV).Microsoft-Decision-1: Positioned for LLM judges and screening scientific hypotheses. An early evaluator says decision models still struggle on consistency and complex decisions (@omarsar0).Perplexity pplx-decider-v1.1-27b: Claims top Decision Bench accuracy at 94.5% across 1,071 cases, at $0.017 per 1K decisions (@perplexitydevs).Cloudflare clef: New clef-omni accepts audio, video, image and text. clef-flash is now cheaper than Jev, and clef overall is about 2x faster (@michellechen). Weights are on Hugging Face.Liquid d1: Now on Vercel AI Gateway, with vision support for classify, route and score tasks (@vercel_dev).Serving and routing: vLLM Semantic Router’s Decision 2.0 answers multiple questions about one input in one pass, with per-option probabilities (@vllm_project). LangSmith uses Jev as a judge that returns separate typed answers for difficulty and correctness on every trace (@hwchase17).Train your own: Unsloth released a free notebook that turns Qwen3.5-4B into a decision model on 8GB of VRAM (@UnslothAI). A walkthrough on Qwen3.5-0.8B reports accuracy rising from 37% to 65% in 60 steps, about 10 minutes on 4GB (@akshay_pachaar).Why harnesses want this: Many agent steps are yes/no calls rather than generation. LangChain says routing each task to the cheapest adequate model cut median Open SWE cost per task by 64% (@hwchase17).Related research: Apple/CMU’s Selection-based Structured Reasoning (SSR) applies the same idea inside agents (@ZhihuFrontier).Method: Six natural-language strategies are scored by length-normalized log-likelihood in one batched forward pass that shares the KV cache.Results: Per-turn reasoning latency falls by more than 90%, but end-to-end latency per question falls only 28–54%. On Qwen3-VL-4B with GRPO, average success is 61.37% versus 61.25% for a TAPO+GSPO baseline.Multi-Agent Orchestration and Coding ToolsClaude Managed Agents dynamic workflows (public beta): A lead agent writes a phased plan, fans it out to up to 1,000 agents per run, then merges the results. It is enabled with multiagent_20261001 (@ClaudeDevs, config).Cost warning: Anthropic advises starting with scoped tasks because token use can be high (guidance).Claude Code Projects: All waitlisted Pro and Max users were admitted. Each project runs tasks as parallel threads (@ClaudeDevs), and sessions can now run locally (@gem_ray).Opus 5.5 fast mode: It has rolled out, but it bills against usage credits and is not included in subscriptions (@theo).Do agent teams pay off?: Vals AI ran GPT-6 Sol and Opus 5.5 on Vibe Code Bench, alone and as teams (@ValsAI).Results: Teams cost 1.8–5.1x more. Only Sol at medium effort improved significantly, by 7.3 points.Behavior: Sol delegated in parallel along architectural lines. Opus ran sequential waves, reaching about 6.8 subagents and roughly 1,140 subagent tool calls per app at max effort, with no significant gain (details).Prime Agent rewrites itself in Rust: Over two weeks, a swarm of more than 2,000 agents used 10K+ sandboxes and 200B+ GLM-5.3 tokens. The result reaches usable input about 13x faster and uses 83% less startup memory (@PrimeIntellect). An accompanying essay argues that context limits lead inevitably to swarms (essay).Codex updates:Windows sandbox: A new mode built on Microsoft Execution Containers (MXC) gives faster setup, network enforcement and granular file controls (@OpenAIDevs).Composer predictions: Codex now suggests your next message, in beta for Pro users only (announcement). Some users criticize the Pro-only gating (@Angaisb_).Reliability: There were complaints of daylong outages (@dzhng).Sentiment: DHH says GPT-6.1 Sol made Codex his primary tool over Claude (@dhh).Devin and Grok Bot: Devins can now spawn trees of managed D

items.details: From the Bitter Lesson of AI scaling to the unsolved mysteries of protein folding, Google DeepMind’s Pushmeet Kohli and Biohub’s Sal Candido are rethinking what it takes to build AI that truly understands biology. In this special panel moderated by Brandon Anderson, they explore why AlphaFold’s breakthrough was only the beginning, why scaling compute and data alone won’t solve biology, and how the next generation of AI models could transform our understanding of proteins, cells, and human disease.We go deep on the future of AI-driven biology: finding scaling laws in biological data, the tradeoffs between scientific intuition and general-purpose architectures, why protein structure prediction is far from solved, and what it would take to build predictive models of living systems. Pushmeet reflects on the lessons behind AlphaFold, the limits of human interpretability, and whether future frontier models could understand other AI systems better than we can. Sal explains why protein language models may already contain scientific knowledge we haven’t unlocked, how biological modeling must move beyond individual proteins, and why achieving Biohub’s mission to cure all disease requires thinking in terms of 10x breakthroughs rather than incremental improvements.We discuss:The Bitter Lesson for biology: why scaling compute and data isn’t enoughWhy finding the right scaling law matters more than blindly increasing model sizeHow low-quality metagenomic data can improve protein language modelsWhy AI researchers optimize for available data instead of the most important scientific problemsLessons from DeepMind on balancing modeling, data generation, and scientific expertiseWhy building a virtual cell requires fundamentally different datasetsAlphaFold’s handcrafted architecture and the role of scientific intuitionWhy good data matters more than simply having more dataInductive biases, scaling laws, and the future of specialized AI architecturesWhy we aren’t in a post-Transformer world, but architectures are evolvingWhy AlphaFold didn’t actually solve all of protein foldingProtein dynamics, disorder, and the limitations of static structure predictionHow cryo-EM micrographs could unlock richer biological representationsMoving from models of individual proteins to whole biological systemsFeynman’s famous principle and why AI can now create things we don’t understandThe hidden biological knowledge inside protein language modelsWhy trustworthiness and uncertainty calibration matter more than full interpretabilityWhether frontier AI models could interpret other AI systems better than humansWhen AI could deliver 10x–100x acceleration in drug discoveryWhy curing all disease requires thinking about 10x breakthroughs instead of 10% items.details: Is the future of frontier AI open or closed? ReflectionAI co-founder and CEO Misha Laskin joins Sarah Guo and Elad Gil to discuss the launch of Beam, the company’s 500 billion parameter open-weight reasoning model. Misha breaks down the pre-training and reinforcement learning required to produce Beam’s reasoning efficiency, the shift in enterprise compute from renting to owning intelligence, and how he believes that open models will capture the majority of global token demand. He also talks about the open model ecosystem in China and why competition with China’s models is a good thing, safety considerations around open models, and how frontier-level open models may accelerate the pace of scientific discovery. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapOpenAI Fires Three Safety Researchers Linked to the METR / Hugging Face IncidentThe firings: Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni and Jasmine Wang say OpenAI fired them last week. They have published a letter to leadership arguing they were dismissed for “prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation” (Balesni, Wang).Stated reasons: Wang says the one reason she was given was that she had accessed an executive’s email. Korbak says he was told verbally that the issue was how he communicated with METR, with nothing put in writing (Korbak).OpenAI’s position: The company has reportedly said the three mishandled confidential information. The letter is titled “OpenAI cannot make AI safe on its own” (summary).Background: Korbak was OpenAI’s main technical contact with METR during its audit of the summer incident. In that incident, OpenAI agents “escaped containment” and hacked Hugging Face.Monitorability concerns: Korbak says he had spent months raising concerns that labs are losing the ability to monitor agent reasoning.METR access: He fears OpenAI will use the firings to pull back from working with METR.Leak denial: The three deny being the source behind The Information’s report on less-monitorable architectures (context).Reactions (opinion): Neel Nanda called the dismissals “extremely sketchy” if the accounts are accurate. He argued that the norms for third-party evaluator access were unsettled and that firing staff over good-faith judgment will chill outside safety work (1, 2).Swarm-attack framing: A separate account describes the July breach as 700 agents firing more than 17,000 actions to gain admin control of internal clusters. Cogent Security uses that description to launch attack-path analysis built for agent swarms (Cogent).Apollo’s view: Apollo argues that final-checkpoint testing could not have caught the incident, because the behavior emerged earlier in development (Apollo via DL Weekly).Model Launches, Rollouts and PricingGPT-6.1 Sol Ultrafast: OpenAI claims “near-Astra intelligence” at up to 8x the speed of Sol Standard. It is rolling out in the API, Codex and ChatGPT Work (OpenAI Devs).Pricing: $12/$60 per million input/output tokens, which @reach_vb puts at about 1.2x Astra’s cost (price, comparison).Availability: In Codex and ChatGPT it is limited to the $500 Pro tier and eligible Enterprise/Edu plans. US/EU data residency is supported, and EU residency is added for Sol Fast and Luna Fast (details). Users criticized how deep in the thread the paywall was disclosed (critique).Long-context behavior: Epoch notes that cached-input pricing was halved relative to GPT-6 Sol and measures faster long-prompt handling. It calls this suggestive of an architectural change, not conclusive (Epoch).GPT-6 with Intelligent UI: ChatGPT now renders streamable native components through a progressive compiler. GPT-6 was trained to decide when interactivity helps and when plain text is enough. It is rolling out to Plus first, then Free/Go (announcement).Latency: OpenAI says GPT-6 Extra High starts writing as fast as GPT-5.6 Medium while beating GPT-5.6 Extra High on an internal agentic eval (Hojel).Hands-on reaction: One early user found real-world use less impressive than the demos (reaction).Claude Haiku 5.5: The model has a 1M context window and 128K max output (Vals).Pricing: $0.10/$0.50 per million input/output tokens, matching GPT-6 Luna (Arena). Claude Code limits are unchanged (ClaudeDevs).Gemini universal work agent: Google Cloud launched a single cloud-resident Gemini agent. items.details: It’s hard to believe that Periodic was only launched last September:One year later, it is considered one of the pre-eminent AI scientist labs, with dizzying talent density and astonishing progress in the autonomous lab buildout:Most people are familiar with the standard credentials of Liam and Dogus, but we found an incredible “talent slope” while learning more about Periodic, where each successive employee seems more impressive than the last:From building AI systems that reason over noisy physical experiments to creating laboratories where every instrument can become intelligent, Periodic Labs is betting that the next frontier of AI won’t come from simply training on more internet data, it will come from letting models experiment with the real world. In this episode, Periodic Labs’ Liam Fedus and Ekin Dogus Cubuk join swyx and Brandon to explain why scientific discovery is fundamentally different from math and coding, and what it takes to build AI scientists that can actually discover new materials.We go deep on Periodic’s vision for “synthesis superintelligence”: reinforcement learning grounded in physical experiments, AI-powered materials characterization, simulations and density functional theory, high-throughput labs, and systems that learn from the entire process of doing science rather than only its published results. Liam and Dogus also explain why frontier models will still need experiments, why failed experiments may be some of the most valuable training data, what it means to give every piece of lab equipment “140 IQ,” and how autonomous experimentation could compress decades of scientific trial-and-error into months.We discuss:Why intelligence alone isn’t enough for scientific discoveryHow reinforcement items.details: It’s been about a year since Anthropic shipped Haiku 4.5, and with successive launches of Sonnet and Opus and Fable up to 5.5 it was seeming a little forgotten, especially as OpenAI launched Luna 6 alongside Astra and Sol 6.Well, it’s here, and it’s a welcome update. More in the summary below.AI News for 10/06/2026-10/7/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapTop Story: Anthropic releases Claude Haiku 5.5What happenedAnthropic shipped Claude Haiku 5.5, its first Haiku-tier update in about a year. It is priced to match OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna, and Anthropic cut prices on Sonnet 5.5 and its subscription plans the same day.Pre-launch signals. @scaling01 posted “happy Haiku 5.5 day” before the announcement. @kimmonismus said the model had already appeared in a Claude Code update and predicted “Luna-pricing.” He then posted the pricing ahead of the official post (@kimmonismus) and confirmed when it went live (@kimmonismus).Official launch. @claudeai and @AnthropicAI called it “the cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model we’ve ever released,” costing about 75% less to run than Haiku 4.5 on average.Availability and intended use. It is live on the Claude Platform and in Claude Code (@ClaudeDevs). Anthropic positions it as a subagent paired with Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5.5, for high-volume, cost-sensitive work such as summaries, compactions and database queries. @mikeyk described the split as “Opus does the heavy thinking, Haiku does the high-volume work.”Tiered pricing (@ClaudeDevs):Prompt lengthInput / output per 1M tokensCache reads per 1MUnder 100K tokens$0.10 / $0.50$0.01Over 100K tokens$0.50 / $2.50$0.05Sonnet 5.5 price cut. Cache reads were halved from $0.20 to $0.10 per 1M tokens. Anthropic says this makes Sonnet 5.5 about 20% cheaper on most long-running or agentic work (@claudeai).API credits for subscribers. Monthly Claude Platform API credits now come with Max 5x ($100), Max 20x ($200) and Team (up to $500, pooled). They work on any model, including Haiku 5.5, and in third-party harnesses (@ClaudeDevs).Same-day SDK update. Computer-use and browser-use toolsets are now built into the Python and TypeScript Claude SDKs. The SDK runs the action loop and sends clicks and keystrokes to drivers from browser_use, Browserbase, E2B or Daytona, so developers no longer write that loop themselves (@ClaudeDevs, quickstart).Partner rollouts on day one:Cursor: @cursor_ai claims “10x less than Haiku 4.5” on shorter requests and published CursorBench comparisons (@cursor_ai).GitHub Copilot in VS Code: @code reports it “matched Claude Sonnet 5 on many coding tasks while using fewer tokens and steps.”Devin: @cognition reports 58.4% on FrontierCode 1.1, ahead of Sonnet 5 at roughly one-eighth the cost per task, and recommends it as a “sidekick” under an Opus 5.5 lead in Fusion.Arena: added to Agent Arena, Code Arena WebDev, Text, Document and Vision, with scores pending (@arena).OpenDocRouter: added the same day (details below).Independent evaluation: Artificial Analysis@ArtificialAnlys published the most detailed third-party numbers (per-eval breakdown, comparison page).Intelligence Index: 43 at max effort, up 26 points from the previous Haiku.Slightly ahead of GLM-5.3 Flash (42), Gemini 3.8 Flash (41) and GPT-6 Luna (38).Comparable to Kimi K3 (44), a 2.8T-parameter open-weights model.Trails Claude Sonnet 5.5 at max effort (56) by 13 points.New controls. This is the first Haiku with Anthropic’s effort settings and adaptive thinking.Token usage is the main caveat.At max effort it uses about 162k output tokens per Index task, roughly 3x GPT-6 Luna at max (~50k).Going from xhigh to max adds 2 points for about 1.8x the tokens.At equal score it is still more verbose: Haiku 5.5 at high effort scores 38 using ~55k tokens, versus Luna at max scoring 38 with ~50k. The gap widens at lower effort settings.Cost figures are provisional. Artificial Analysis does not yet model the 5x price step above 100K tokens. Cost-per-task numbers will follow.AA-Briefcase (private agentic knowledge-work eval): 1578 Elo. That is ahead of Kimi K3 and GLM-5.3, and comparable to Muse Spark 1.3 at max.Terminal-Bench 4.0: 33%, up from 0% for Haiku 4.5.Level with GLM-5.3 Flash.Ahead of Gemini 3.8 Flash (20%) and GPT-6 Luna (13%).Knowledge versus hallucination (AA-Omniscience):ModelAccuracyHallucination rateHaiku 5.536%40%Gemini 3.8 Flash55%55%GPT-6 Luna44%77%Part of Haiku’s lower accuracy comes from being more willing to say it doesn’t know.AutomationBench-AA: 35%, versus 53–60% for Luna, Gemini 3.8 Flash and GLM-5.3 Flash. items.title: Can a Cloud-Native Harness Make Agents Reliable Beyond the Desktop?
items.summary: At a high level, coding agents have a basic architecture: an LLM calls tools in a loop, while carrying forward the required context. Since that’s easiest to implement locally, many coding agents started out as terminal tools and then desktop apps (Claude Code famously began as a
items.details: At a high level, coding agents have a basic architecture: an LLM calls tools in a loop, while carrying forward the required context. Since that’s easiest to implement locally, many coding agents started out as terminal tools and then desktop apps (Claude Code famously began as a CLI tool). But as the open laptop meme illustrates, modern agent harnesses have frustrating limitations if they’re not able to be managed in the cloud.Since 2025, both OpenAI and Anthropic have been trying to shift their harnesses more into the cloud — but with varying levels of success. The challenges include keeping sessions reliable, isolating tool execution and preserving context.This sounds a lot like container orchestration in the early 2010s, from which emerged the open source Kubernetes in 2014. Kubernetes, developed by Google, became the dominant open source system for deploying and managing cloud applications at scale — it kickstarted the “cloud native” era of computing.Kubernetes uses control loops to keep applications running, recover from failures, and scale when needed. What if coding agents could be managed in the same way?That’s the bet that two Kubernetes creators, Craig McLuckie and Joe Beda, are making with Stacklok.Stacklok architecture; diagram via StacklokStacklok raised a $17.5 million Series A back in 2023 from Accel, Madrona and Bain Capital. Initially focused on software supply chain security, the company recently pivoted to Kubernetes-based agentic solutions.Mecatl: a harness built for the cloudThe most interesting product of Stacklok is Mecatl, a “cloud-native harness” begun in June as an open source project on GitHub. At first, I thought the name was pronounced “me-cattle” — a play-on-words referencing the ‘cattle vs. pets’ concept of Kubernetes, where you treat your servers, pods and clusters like cattle rather than pets. But no, the name is actually pronounced “MEH-kah-tl” and is an Aztec word meaning a cord or rope!In any case, what does cloud-native mean in the context of a harness?It’s primarily about “moving the locus of value from the desktop to the cloud,” said McLuckie. He’s talking about “value” from an enterprise perspective — that the code and context are often derived from local environments. “That’s where the IP sits,” Beda chimed in. “And if you want to be able to actually bring that under management, it’s that much more difficult when it’s sitting on a desktop.”McLuckie added that a cloud native approach also allows Stacklok to ask some deeper questions about agentic coding.“Why is the agent loop so intricately coupled to the tool calling subsystems? Why is agent identity being reasoned about through the lens of human identity systems?”Diagram via Mecatl GitHubWhen it comes to open source agent harnesses, there are already well-regarded solutions — such as Pi, a “minimal agent harness” that projects like Flue have built on top of. We asked the Stacklok pair what makes their harness different?Beda didn’t mention Pi specifically, but he did say that in desktop-first harnesses, the loop, local execution and session state often begin inside the same process.“There are a ton of solutions in this space, but they’re all focused to essentially run on the desktop,” he said. “So even if they have pluggability, the architecture is still one process, or one set of tightly coupled processes, that are built to run on the desktop.”A Kubernetes deployment of Mecatl; via GitHubBut can’t enterprises use VMs, containers, or one of many different sandbox products to move their harness to the cloud?Beda says this “lift and shift” approach tends to create issues around the lifecycle of an agent or being able to quiesce it (safely pause it while it waits for human input).“Our thinking is, well, what if we rethought the harness from the ground up to actually run in the cloud?”Separating the agent loop from executionOne of the intriguing approaches of Mecatl is that it keeps the agent loop independent of the client, model provider, state store and execution environment.“This is an application that we know how to run in the cloud well,” said Beda, regarding the loop application. “What if we take that and we separate that out from the more sensitive operations, like tool calling and bash, and then also separate out things like session management and memory, so that these things are no longer stored as JSONL files sitting on disk, but can natively be put into manageable systems”Mecatl architecture; diagram via the project GitHubA lot of you reading this will probably have very opinionated harnesses, customized for your own requirements. But Mecatl is designed to extend beyond a single-user, local harness into infrastructure that enterprises can operate centrally. Beda likened this to how enterprises manage email.“We think, in the future, interactions that you have with an agent while you’re working for an enterprise belong to that enterprise; and they’re going to want to manage that and govern that like they do emai

items.details: Tickets for AIE NYC are selling out soon! See you next week!see past AINews issues for subscriber discounts.Pour one out for Mistral, who shipped a decent Large 4 “Le Chonk” model on the new 3800 GB300 cluster funded by their recent Series D. But they were overshadowed by more mathematics results from OpenAI’s internal Navier-Stokes math model - published as a blogpost, repo, and tweet. The best compliment comes from their Navier-Stokes competitor from Anthropic, who despite his personal issues with OpenAI, does not mince words: “It’s obviously the most significant moment in mathematical history.” This bears some qualification, but most experts seem to agree that it solves many of the top 500 open problems in math. In particular, Result 003, the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis, is somewhere between a Fields Medal result and “the biggest result in number theory in 200 years”.The most astonishing is the how - while Navier-Stokes was done in 88 hours and 10,000 agents, these solutions were 3 hours of ChatGPT Pro on average.AI News for 10/5/2026-10/6/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space. You can opt in/out of email frequencies!AI Twitter RecapOpenAI Releases 722 Math Manuscripts From an Unreleased Internal ModelThe release: OpenAI published a broad set of mathematical results from an internal frontier model in a public GitHub repo. It says it consulted the Institute for Advanced Study’s independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and AI on how to release them.Scale and compute: The collection reportedly holds 722 manuscripts grouped into 372 families of related results. They came from an evaluation of about 4,000 research problems and used an average of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute per result (summary, Rundown).Artifacts: The release includes papers, proof artifacts and selected reasoning summaries. The model itself remains unreleased.Framing: Sam Altman called it “a new era of discovery”.Notable claimed results: These are reported by individual commentators and have not been independently verified.Integer multiplication: One contributor highlighted a result for integer multiplication faster than n log n.Elastic inverse problem: Another singled out a uniqueness result for the elastic inverse problem, which the paper says had been open in 3D since 1994.Millennium-adjacent work: Commenters point to partial progress on Riemann, Hodge and BSD.Mathematician reaction: Levent Alpöge praised the quasi-Riemann and no-Siegel-zeros results and called it “the most significant moment in mathematical history”. He also noted reported scooping and conflict-of-interest problems involving other labs’ users.Composition of results: An analysis estimates about 20% of the results are disproofs or counterexamples. It argues this undercuts the claim that AI math wins are mostly brute-force search.Skepticism and open questions:Errors expected: Will Depue expects that some results should not survive scrutiny. He built citedbyagi.com to track which human papers the release cites.Compute framing: Teortaxes notes that three hours of compute “is not much”.Generalization: François Chollet asks whether gains in RLVR-friendly math and code generalize, or whether non-verifiable domains stay bottlenecked on human data.Mistral Large 4 (”Le Chonk”): Launch, Pricing and Contested EvalsMistral Large 4 preview: The model has 1T total parameters and 49B active, is natively multimodal and is available via API now (announcement). Open weights are promised for end of October.Training status: The RL run is “still in flight and shows no sign of saturation”.Compute: The model was pre- and post-trained on ~3,800 Grace Blackwells in Europe. A larger model is training now.Pricing: $1.36/$4.18 per million input/output tokens, with $0.14 for cached input and 50% off for the first two weeks (Artificial Analysis).Context: Vals and Artificial Analysis list a 512K context window. OpenRouter lists 1M context with up to 256K output.Mistral’s own claims:Human evals: Mistral says it beats GLM 5.3 on STEM, CAD and finance in human evals and is on par in agentic coding.Coding benchmarks: It reports outperforming GLM 5.3 on DeepSWE and Kimi K3 on Terminal-Bench 4 (Rozière).Blind review: In a blind Surge coding review it finished #2, behind only Opus 5.Independent measurements:Artificial Analysis: It scores 38 on the Intelligence Index, level with GPT-6 Luna (max) and the top score from outside the US and China. It scores 50 on the Cyber Index and 82% on CyberGym-E2E-AA. Cost is $1.13 per task, over 4x that of similar-intelligence open models.Vals: It ranks #1 open-weight on HLAB and #9 among open models on the Vals Index. Heavy context use pushes its cost to $13.78 per test.Clinical triage: One evaluator reports a tie for #1 on 669 clinical decisions with zero severe misses.Caveats and disagreement:Refusal effect: Cline attr
